children.text: A new Census Bureau report found that U.S. Latinos were three times more likely to live in poverty than the general population, with nearly a third of Hispanics below the poverty line. Latino/as made up 18% of the nation's poor despite representing only 9% of the population, and almost half of the poor Latino/as were children under 18. Cuban-American activists in Miami and New York protested the Mexican government's decision to deport a boatload of Cuban refugees who had been at sea for 21 days after their vessel suffered mechanical problems near Cancun. Ten people died during the journey, including two children. The Clinton administration appeared before the U.S. Court of Appeals to challenge a lower-court ruling that blocked NAFTA from going to Congress until an environmental impact study was completed. At a border summit in El Paso, Texas, Congressman Ron Coleman argued it was unfair to impose special taxes on border businesses to pay for NAFTA-related infrastructure, comparing the situation to not charging Mississippi River communities for flood damage. A separate community summit in Tijuana brought together U.S. and Mexican labor and environmental groups who argued that NAFTA, as negotiated, served corporate interests rather than workers or communities.
Homestead, Florida: One Year After Hurricane Andrew

Correspondent Emilio San Pedro reported from the Florida City and Homestead area of South Dade County on the first anniversary of Hurricane Andrew. While some larger agricultural businesses had resumed operations and Florida Governor Lawton Chiles visited to mark progress, many farmworkers remained far from recovered. The Centro Campesino, a farmworker support organization, had helped build over 60 homes through a sweat equity program, but housing costs had risen sharply following the destruction of most local trailer parks and apartments. Lemon and lime groves and plant nurseries, which had employed many year-round workers, were largely wiped out. Federal disaster assistance from FEMA was described as short-term and inadequate, covering personal belongings but not long-term housing or employment needs. A young student named Raul described how his family stayed despite losing their restaurant business on the very day their insurance was to be approved.
Orchard Beach: The Puerto Rican Riviera

Correspondent Mandalit del Barco produced a sound portrait of Orchard Beach in the Bronx, a free outdoor destination that Latino New Yorkers, especially Puerto Ricans, had claimed as their summer escape. Beachgoers described it as their version of Cancun or Puerto Rico, a place where people from across the Latino diaspora gathered for salsa and merengue concerts, family reunions, and a break from the stress of project living and street violence. The water itself was widely acknowledged as too polluted to swim in, but the boardwalk, the music, and the company were enough to make it a beloved institution.
Gonzalo Rubalcaba Makes His U.S. Debut

Correspondent Alfredo Cruz reported on Cuban jazz pianist Gonzalo Rubalcaba's historic first U.S. performance at Lincoln Center in May, the result of years of negotiations with the State Department. Rubalcaba, considered one of Cuba's premier pianists and the son of a celebrated Cuban bandleader, had been denied a performance visa for years on political grounds. American bassist Charlie Haden, who had heard Rubalcaba at the 1989 Montreux Jazz Festival, worked with Blue Note Records and Lincoln Center to secure the visa. Rubalcaba was permitted to play only one concert and on the condition that he receive no payment. The performance was viewed by many in both countries as a potential cultural icebreaker in U.S.-Cuba relations.

Performance artist and Latino USA commentator Guillermo Gomez-Pena proposed a cultural parallel to NAFTA, which he called a Free Art Agreement. Rather than the exchange of goods, this framework would facilitate the exchange of ideas, aesthetics, and values across the Americas. He argued that Mexican and Caribbean cultures could offer political intelligence and community-based resilience to the North, while North American artists could offer Latin America discourse on race, gender, and experimentation. Gomez-Pena cautioned that well-intentioned Anglo or European collaborators often unconsciously replicated colonial dynamics, and called for genuine power-sharing and ongoing dialogue as the foundation for any cross-cultural creative partnership.
